title: Cold Mountain
hookLine: the hermit poet Han Shan wrote poems on rocks and trees
tomorrow: a guest feels too dusty to sit down. what does Love say?

lines: A LINE ON A PARK BENCH.
cards: Sticky notes on a fridge, a message chalked on a sidewalk, a line scratched into a park bench: people still write where anyone might find it.

Tradition says a hermit called Han Shan, Cold Mountain, wrote his poems on rocks, on trees, on the walls of village houses, for whoever passed. Later an official went looking and copied down what he could find.
So who were the poems for? Anyone. Which turns out to include us.

teach.b: Han Shan took his name from his mountain, and the poems blur the two. People ask the way to Cold Mountain, he writes; there's no road that gets through. If your heart were like mine, you'd arrive.
So here's the debate inside Chan Buddhism: is Cold Mountain a place you go, or a mind you have?
View one: go up. Han Shan's poems praise the hermit life, the clouds, the cold, the freedom from status and money. The best case: some clarity only comes when you actually leave the noise behind.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: BACK TO THE MARKET.
teach.b: View two: come back down. The Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, a Chan teaching told in pictures, follow a seeker who finds and tames an ox, his own mind.
And the last picture isn't a mountaintop. He walks into the marketplace with open hands.

The best case: an awakening that never comes down the mountain helps nobody. And Han Shan himself? Tradition says he came down too, to a temple kitchen, where he and his friend Shide laughed together over the leftovers.
Maybe the rocks are part of the answer: he went up, and still left words beside the road.

how: Chan and Zen Buddhists read Han Shan's poems and the Ten Ox-Herding Pictures side by side: the hermit's mountain and the return to the marketplace with open hands.

o: a winter festival held on the highest peak around
Han Shan's mountain, his name, and his state of mind
a monastery where monks fasted through the cold

games.q: up the mountain, back to town: tap the pairs.
p: laughed with him in a temple kitchen
back to the market with open hands

s: Han Shan's poems were first written down in a book
tradition says on rocks, trees and walls; an official copied them later.
the last Ox-Herding Picture shows the seeker back in the marketplace
he returns to town with open hands.
Cold Mountain is only the name of a real mountain
it's his home and his name, and in the poems a mind with no road to it.

games.q: you think going off-grid to find clarity is selfish. what's the strongest case for the other side, from today?
o: some clarity only comes when you leave the noise, and Han Shan still left words for others.
it's fine because nobody really needs you anyway.
hermits owe nothing to anyone, so there's no harm in it.
games.why: the best case for going up is clarity, and Han Shan's mountain still sent poems down to the road.

practice: Write one short kind line by hand, on a sticky note or the back of a receipt: thank you, you're doing fine, the light is nice here. Hold it while you sit.
Later, it could go somewhere a stranger might find it, the way Han Shan's did.
